history.heading: The Rock of Polynesia
paragraphs: Niue, one of the world's largest raised coral islands, lies in the South Pacific east of Tonga. It was settled by Polynesians from Samoa and Tonga about 1,000 years ago or more. Captain James Cook, unable to land in 1774 because of hostile reception, called it "Savage Island".

Christian missionaries arrived in the 19th century. Niue became a British protectorate in 1900 and was annexed to New Zealand in 1901. It became self-governing in free association with New Zealand in 1974. Cyclone Heta caused severe damage in 2004.

culture.heading: Island life
paragraphs: Niuean and English are spoken. Most people are Christian, and church is central to community life. Only about 1,700 people live on Niue, while over 30,000 Niueans live in New Zealand. Traditional ceremonies include hair-cutting and ear-piercing rites for children.

politics.heading: Free association
paragraphs: Niue is a self-governing state in free association with New Zealand. Niueans are New Zealand citizens. It has its own parliament (Fono Ekepule) and premier. New Zealand assists with defence and foreign affairs on request, though Niue conducts its own diplomacy with many countries.

economy.heading: Small economy
paragraphs: Niue's economy depends heavily on New Zealand aid, tourism, fishing licences and selling postage stamps and coins to collectors. It has been a pioneer in ocean conservation, protecting 40 percent of its waters and selling "ocean conservation commitments". The currency is the New Zealand dollar.
